youtube.aciklama:
What are the most common causes of dizziness in children, and how are vestibular tests adapted for a child? In this lesson we cover the criteria for vestibular migraine of childhood and recurrent vertigo of childhood, red flags, motor development, an age-appropriate test battery, and vestibular assessment in children with hearing loss and implant candidates.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; van de Berg et al., Vestibular migraine of childhood and recurrent vertigo of childhood: Diagnostic criteria, Journal of Vestibular Research (2021).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the main causes of dizziness in children and how vestibular assessment is adapted for a child.
We will cover vestibular migraine of childhood, motor development, and vestibular tests in children with hearing loss or implant candidates.
A young child cannot describe dizziness; families more often see sudden falls, grabbing onto things, pallor or vomiting.
Some children become frightened during attacks and cling to a parent, or want to stay still.
So most of the history comes from the family; the frequency and duration of attacks and the accompanying symptoms are asked in detail.
A short video taken by the family on a phone is very valuable, especially for showing eye movements.
The causes of dizziness in children are distributed differently than in adults; the most common are migraine-related conditions.

cumleler.yazi: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV, and Meniere's disease, common in adults, are less frequent in children.
cumleler.ses: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or B P P V, and Meniere's disease, common in adults, are less frequent in children.

cumleler: In the vestibular migraine lesson we mentioned that there are separate criteria for children.

cumleler.yazi: In 2021 the Barany Society and the International Headache Society defined two diagnoses for childhood.
cumleler.ses: In twenty twenty one the Barany Society and the International Headache Society defined two diagnoses for childhood.

cumleler.yazi: Vestibular migraine of childhood, or VMC, requires at least five vestibular attacks of moderate or severe intensity.
cumleler.ses: Vestibular migraine of childhood, or V M C, requires at least five vestibular attacks of moderate or severe intensity.

cumleler: Attacks last five minutes to seventy two hours, the child has a history of migraine, and at least half the attacks show migraine features.
These features include a throbbing headache and sensitivity to light and sound.

cumleler.yazi: For recurrent vertigo of childhood, or RVC, at least three attacks are enough, without migraine history or features.
cumleler.ses: For recurrent vertigo of childhood, or R V C, at least three attacks are enough, without migraine history or features.

cumleler.yazi: RVC replaced the condition formerly called benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood; both diagnoses apply under the age of eighteen.
cumleler.ses: R V C replaced the condition formerly called benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood; both diagnoses apply under the age of eighteen.

cumleler: The physician makes the diagnosis; audiological and vestibular tests help rule out other causes and document the picture.
A purely illustrative case: a six-year-old is brought in for spinning attacks that happen a few times a month and last a few minutes.
During attacks the child turns pale and holds on to the mother; between attacks the child is completely well and keeps playing.
The mother has a history of migraine; no clear headache has yet been described in the child.
The audiogram, tympanometry and child-adapted vestibular tests are normal.
This picture may be consistent with recurrent vertigo of childhood; some of these children develop migraine later.
Normal test results are also valuable; the family is informed and asked to keep an attack diary.
Fluid in the middle ear, or otitis media with effusion, is a common and easily missed cause of imbalance and clumsiness in children.

cumleler.yazi: Dizziness is common after head trauma and concussion; BPPV can also occur after trauma.
cumleler.ses: Dizziness is common after head trauma and concussion; B P P V can also occur after trauma.

cumleler: Vestibular neuritis also occurs in children; it usually starts with sudden, constant dizziness after an infection.
Refractive errors and eye muscle imbalance can also cause dizziness and unsteadiness; an eye examination is part of the battery.
Central causes such as posterior fossa tumors are rare, but they must not be missed.
In adolescence, functional conditions such as anxiety-related and persistent perceptual dizziness may also be seen.
Headache that worsens in the morning together with vomiting may suggest raised intracranial pressure.
New problems with walking, speech or eye movements alongside imbalance point to a central problem.
If sudden hearing loss accompanies the dizziness, assessment must not be delayed.
Signs of infection such as fever, ear discharge and neck stiffness also need urgent assessment.
Imbalance that is constant and steadily worsening, rather than coming in attacks, is also referred to a physician quickly.
When the audiologist sees these signs, the child is referred to a physician without delay rather than continuing the tests.
The vestibular system plays a key role in a baby holding the head up, sitting and walking.
Healthy babies can usually hold their heads up at three to four months of age.
Sitting without support usually develops between six and eight months.
Independent walking starts at around twelve months on average; normally this can take a few months longer.
Harder balance skills, such as standing on one foot and hopping, mature in the preschool years.
A clear delay in these milestones is an important clue for vestibular assessment in a baby with hearing loss.
In babies with bilateral vestibular loss, head control, sitting and especially walking may be delayed.
In Usher syndrome type one, for example, congenital hearing loss comes with bilateral vestibular loss; walking often starts after 18 months.
Over time these children learn to rely more on vision and on input from the soles of the feet.
So their balance may get clearly worse in the dark or on soft, uneven ground.
At school age, difficulty with skills such as riding a bike and ball games, and complaints of falls and clumsiness are common.
When vestibular loss is detected early, physiotherapy and support for motor development can be planned.

cumleler.yazi: In infants, the cervical vestibular evoked myogenic potential, or cVEMP, shows saccular function; it is recorded on a lap, head turned.
cumleler.ses: In infants, the cervical vestibular evoked myogenic potential, or C vemp, shows saccular function; it is recorded on a lap, head turned.

cumleler: In the rotary chair, the baby is tested on a parent's lap; we mentioned this in the rotary chair lesson.
In children over three, most of the vestibular tests used in adults can be done.
The video head impulse test, or vHIT, can be done in young children with light goggles; successful infant recordings have been reported.
The caloric test is more unpleasant for a child; it is usually done in older children and at the end of the battery.
At school age, posturography and age-appropriate balance and motor tests complete the picture.
In children, the test order is planned to start with the easiest and least unpleasant test.
In eye movement tests, engaging targets such as cartoon characters are used instead of dots.
VEMP and vHIT are short and painless; they are first introduced to the child as a game.
Balance tests, such as standing on foam or walking along a line, are turned into games.
If a caloric test is needed, it is left until last, so any discomfort does not affect the other tests.
If some tests cannot be done, the result is reported as it is; an incomplete battery can still give valuable information.
In vHIT, the child's head is turned with small, quick movements while a camera built into the goggles records eye movement.
The lateral canals are the easiest to test; the vertical canal pairs are harder in children.
To keep the goggles from slipping, a child-sized frame and a tight strap are used.
The child needs to look at a target on the wall; a favorite picture or a light-up toy can serve as the target.
In young children normal gain is close to adult values, but measurement artifact is more common, so recordings are checked carefully.
Vestibular disorders have been reported in a large share of children with sensorineural hearing loss, about twenty to eighty five percent.
The rate varies with the study and especially with the cause of the loss.
Vestibular involvement is common in losses due to congenital cytomegalovirus infection and after meningitis.
It is also common in syndromes such as Usher syndrome type one, CHARGE syndrome and Pendred syndrome.
Enlarged vestibular aqueduct and other inner ear malformations can also affect vestibular function.
For this reason, vestibular assessment is increasingly recommended for children with severe and profound hearing loss.
In a child who is a cochlear implant candidate, vestibular tests document the vestibular function of both ears before surgery.
Implant surgery may reduce vestibular function to some extent in the operated ear.
So if vestibular function is clearly better in one ear, this information can help the team choose the side.
The aim is to protect the single good ear the child relies on for balance; the decision is made by the surgeon and the team.
The preoperative record provides a basis for comparison if a new complaint arises after surgery.
Giving the family realistic information about the child's motor development and balance is also part of this assessment.

sahneler.metin: Explain the test to the child as a game, keep the parent close and start with the easiest test. If a caloric is needed, leave it until last.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: success in pediatric vestibular testing depends largely on the trust built in the first five minutes.
Explain the test as a game, keep the parent close, and show tools such as the goggles on a toy first.
Start with the easiest test; when the child gets tired or restless, take a break or reschedule rather than forcing it.
A forced test gives unreliable results and also makes later assessments harder.

Adapt the battery to age and child

cumleler: In children the most common causes are migraine-related: vestibular migraine of childhood and recurrent vertigo of childhood.
Delays in head control, sitting and walking are an important clue to vestibular loss in a baby with hearing loss.

cumleler.yazi: The test battery is adapted to age: cVEMP and rotary chair in infants, vHIT and if needed caloric testing in older children.
cumleler.ses: The test battery is adapted to age: C vemp and rotary chair in infants, vHIT and if needed caloric testing in older children.

cumleler: Many children with hearing loss have vestibular disorders; in implant candidates both ears are assessed before surgery.

sahneler.soru: How many attacks does recurrent vertigo of childhood require?
sahneler.aciklama: For RVC, at least three attacks are enough; vestibular migraine of childhood requires at least five attacks and migraine features.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: how many vestibular attacks are needed, at minimum, for a diagnosis of recurrent vertigo of childhood?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: at least three attacks.
Vestibular migraine of childhood, by contrast, requires at least five attacks, with migraine features in at least half of them.
